decisive_item.title: Nvidia GPU Debt Backstop Unleashes the AI Project Trinity: Capital, Offtake and Datacenters
decisive_item.who: Sharon AI (counterparty disclosure, reported by SemiAnalysis)
decisive_item.passage: Sharon disclosed a total backstop value of $4.88B

meaning.what: total value of NVIDIA's backstop on Sharon's 72MW Australian AI factory (up to 40,000 GB300)

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis estimates NVIDIA’s second-half 2026 shipment volumes and revenue above general-market estimates, based on its supply-chain tracking.
passages: Nvidia revenue is skyrocketing, and even 3 years into the build out, the general market is still materially lower on shipment volumes and revenue estimates for Nvidia in the 2nd half of this year versus our through supply chain tracking in the Accelerator Model .

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis reports that NVIDIA has started providing neoclouds take-or-pay minimum-revenue guarantees on GPU capacity, in return for a share of revenue above the guarantee.
passages: This is why Nvidia has stepped in and has started backstopping GPU rental offtakes themselves . In the backstop program, Nvidia provides a take-or-pay commitment to Neoclouds – a minimum revenue guarantee on the underlying GPU capacity. In exchange for this backstop, Nvidia also shares in a portion of the Neocloud’s revenue earned above the backstop level.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis reports that NVIDIA has started backstopping data-center leases as part of its support for neoclouds.
passages: Here, Nvidia is diving even deeper, as it has started backstopping datacenter leases.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis says NVIDIA’s backstops typically run for six years; its illustrative lower-end pricing curve averages $2.36 per GPU-hour over six years, and it expects most neoclouds to negotiate higher backstops.
passages: Nvidia’s backstop program is typically six years in length, and during these six years, Nvidia stands ready to purchase compute at pre-agreed price levels that vary over the time period. Each Neocloud is expected to negotiate the backstop terms individually, and we can expect that different Neoclouds may end up with different revenue share and backstop schedules. The below table is an illustrative example to explain the basic terms of the program – we present a backstop pricing curve that we believe to be on the lower end of the backstop range – in this case at an average of $2.36 over the six-year period, but we expect that most Neoclouds will negotiate higher backstops.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis models a 25.4% project IRR for a neocloud’s one-year rental-book scenario with an NVIDIA backstop, the highest return among the backstopped scenarios it analyzed.
passages: We see that the short-term 1y rental book scenario clearly offers the best IRR among the backstopped scenarios at 25.4%, and these IRRs could realize even higher if the rental market turns out to be strong enough such that 1y and shorter rental rates decay by less than we modeled in the curve below.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis says banks underwriting NVIDIA-backstopped GPU financing seek at least 1.3x debt-service coverage, typically corresponding to 70–80% loan-to-value, especially in the first years.
passages: When it comes to the Nvidia backstop, banks look at the DSCR ratios assuming revenue earned under the scenario where the backstop is activated. They are looking for a DSCR of at least 1.3x, particularly for the first few years of GPU financing agreement and size their loans to ensure that this bar is met. This typically corresponds to a 70-80% loan to value (LTV) ratio.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis expects initial lending for NVIDIA-backstopped GPU financing to price wider than hyperscaler-backstopped deals at about 5.9% yield but tighter than CoreWeave’s roughly 10% unsecured bond yield.
passages: We think that initial lending will be at a wider spread than the current 5y backstopped hyperscale deals which come in at around SOFR + 225bps (roughly equivalent to a Z-spread of 195bps, or about 5.9% total yield) but at a tighter spread than CoreWeave’s 5-year unsecured corporate bond which has a yield of ~10% (roughly equivalent to Z-spread of 600bps).

kept_from_that_article.summary: SharonAI announced a 72MW Australian AI factory backed by NVIDIA for up to 40,000 GB300 GPUs over six years, disclosing $4.88 billion of backstop value, or an implied average floor of about $2.33 per GPU-hour.
passages: The first is SharonAI’s 72MW AI factory in Australia. Announced in June 2026, the deal has SharonAI scaling up to as many as 40,000 GB300s under a six-year backstop. Sharon disclosed a total backstop value of $4.88B, which works out to an implied floor of about $2.33/hr/GPU on average over the six year period.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SharonAI guides to a total fleet of more than 55,000 NVIDIA GPUs by mid-2027, including up to 40,000 backstopped GB300s; its footprint is set to reach 132MW, of which 102MW is contracted.
passages: Sharon AI’s footprint is now set to grow to 132MW with 102MW contracted, and the company guides to reaching more than 55,000 Nvidia GPUs in total (inclusive of the 40,000 GB300s backstopped) by mid-2027.

kept_from_that_article.summary: Firmus announced its 360MW Batam AI cluster project on June 29, 2026, as part of NVIDIA’s backstop program.
passages: Announced just recently on June 29 th , 2026, this project shows the scale at which Nvidia is rolling out the backstop program.

kept_from_that_article.summary: Firmus expects $25 billion to $30 billion of customer revenue over six years for the Batam cluster project.
passages: Firmus announced that they expect $25B to $30B of customer revenue over the six years.

kept_from_that_article.summary: Firmus announced a 600MW firm-energy deal with Gunvor that will underwrite 1.2GW of new renewables development and 1.5GWh of storage in South Australia by 2032.
passages: Beyond this – Firmus also announced a 600MW firm-energy deal with Gunvor that will also underwrite 1.2GW of new renewables development and 1.5GWh of storage in South Australia by 2032.

kept_from_that_article.summary: CoreWeave paid a 5.9% yield on the fixed-rate tranche of its $8.5 billion DDTL 4.0 delayed-draw term loan backed by Meta, about 90 basis points wider than Meta’s roughly 5.0% five-year bond yield; CoreWeave’s five-year unsecured bonds yielded about 10%.
passages: Readers may notice the huge gap between CoreWeave 5y unsecured bonds at ~10% and the 5.9% that CoreWeave paid for the fixed-rate tranche of their DDTL 4.0 $8.5B delayed-draw term loan, which was backstopped by Meta. This 5.9% yield works out to about 90 basis points wider than Meta’s 5y bond yield of ~5.0%.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis estimates NVIDIA’s second-half 2026 shipment volumes and revenue above general-market estimates, based on its supply-chain tracking.
passages: Nvidia revenue is skyrocketing, and even 3 years into the build out, the general market is still materially lower on shipment volumes and revenue estimates for Nvidia in the 2nd half of this year versus our through supply chain tracking in the Accelerator Model .

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis reports that NVIDIA has started providing neoclouds take-or-pay minimum-revenue guarantees on GPU capacity, in return for a share of revenue above the guarantee.
passages: This is why Nvidia has stepped in and has started backstopping GPU rental offtakes themselves . In the backstop program, Nvidia provides a take-or-pay commitment to Neoclouds – a minimum revenue guarantee on the underlying GPU capacity. In exchange for this backstop, Nvidia also shares in a portion of the Neocloud’s revenue earned above the backstop level.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis reports that NVIDIA has started backstopping data-center leases as part of its support for neoclouds.
passages: Here, Nvidia is diving even deeper, as it has started backstopping datacenter leases.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis says NVIDIA’s backstops typically run for six years; its illustrative lower-end pricing curve averages $2.36 per GPU-hour over six years, and it expects most neoclouds to negotiate higher backstops.
passages: Nvidia’s backstop program is typically six years in length, and during these six years, Nvidia stands ready to purchase compute at pre-agreed price levels that vary over the time period. Each Neocloud is expected to negotiate the backstop terms individually, and we can expect that different Neoclouds may end up with different revenue share and backstop schedules. The below table is an illustrative example to explain the basic terms of the program – we present a backstop pricing curve that we believe to be on the lower end of the backstop range – in this case at an average of $2.36 over the six-year period, but we expect that most Neoclouds will negotiate higher backstops.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis models a 25.4% project IRR for a neocloud’s one-year rental-book scenario with an NVIDIA backstop, the highest return among the backstopped scenarios it analyzed.
passages: We see that the short-term 1y rental book scenario clearly offers the best IRR among the backstopped scenarios at 25.4%, and these IRRs could realize even higher if the rental market turns out to be strong enough such that 1y and shorter rental rates decay by less than we modeled in the curve below.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis says banks underwriting NVIDIA-backstopped GPU financing seek at least 1.3x debt-service coverage, typically corresponding to 70–80% loan-to-value, especially in the first years.
passages: When it comes to the Nvidia backstop, banks look at the DSCR ratios assuming revenue earned under the scenario where the backstop is activated. They are looking for a DSCR of at least 1.3x, particularly for the first few years of GPU financing agreement and size their loans to ensure that this bar is met. This typically corresponds to a 70-80% loan to value (LTV) ratio.

kept_from_that_article.summary: SemiAnalysis expects initial lending for NVIDIA-backstopped GPU financing to price wider than hyperscaler-backstopped deals at about 5.9% yield but tighter than CoreWeave’s roughly 10% unsecured bond yield.
passages: We think that initial lending will be at a wider spread than the current 5y backstopped hyperscale deals which come in at around SOFR + 225bps (roughly equivalent to a Z-spread of 195bps, or about 5.9% total yield) but at a tighter spread than CoreWeave’s 5-year unsecured corporate bond which has a yield of ~10% (roughly equivalent to Z-spread of 600bps).

kept_from_that_article.summary: SharonAI announced a 72MW Australian AI factory backed by NVIDIA for up to 40,000 GB300 GPUs over six years, disclosing $4.88 billion of backstop value, or an implied average floor of about $2.33 per GPU-hour.

passages: Sharon AI’s footprint is now set to grow to 132MW with 102MW contracted, and the company guides to reaching more than 55,000 Nvidia GPUs in total (inclusive of the 40,000 GB300s backstopped) by mid-2027.

kept_from_that_article.summary: CoreWeave paid a 5.9% yield on the fixed-rate tranche of its $8.5 billion DDTL 4.0 delayed-draw term loan backed by Meta, about 90 basis points wider than Meta’s roughly 5.0% five-year bond yield; CoreWeave’s five-year unsecured bonds yielded about 10%.

passages: Readers may notice the huge gap between CoreWeave 5y unsecured bonds at ~10% and the 5.9% that CoreWeave paid for the fixed-rate tranche of their DDTL 4.0 $8.5B delayed-draw term loan, which was backstopped by Meta. This 5.9% yield works out to about 90 basis points wider than Meta’s 5y bond yield of ~5.0%.
